claims.text: Greg LaVecchia asserts that paid performance marketing (e.g., Facebook/Meta ads) and influencer marketing are structurally different distribution mechanisms: paid ads force distribution to tens of millions of people via a credit card, while influencer content reaches audiences entirely at the algorithm's discretion. This means the brand cannot control influencer reach the way it controls paid reach.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
claims.mechanism: Paid media routes budget directly to impressions via platform ad auctions; influencer content enters the organic feed and rises or falls based on algorithmic engagement signals, not advertiser spend.

claims.text: Greg LaVecchia asserts that deploying a strict product brief, content brief, or campaign brief to influencers suppresses the reach of influencer marketing content, because viral distribution is determined by the algorithm, not brand messaging directives. When creators are constrained by scripted talking points, their content loses the authenticity and format cues that algorithms reward, reducing views.
claims.speaker: Greg LaVecchia
conditions: Goal is viral reach / maximum views
Working with content creators or influencers on organic/algorithm-distributed content (not paid placement)
claims.mechanism: Algorithms surface content based on creator-native engagement signals (authenticity, format fit, audience resonance); rigid brand scripts override those signals, causing the content to underperform relative to the creator's organic work.
bounded_by: Does not apply to paid influencer placements where reach is purchased regardless of algorithmic performance
Does not apply to paid performance marketing (Facebook/Meta ads) where distribution is bought directly

practices.text: In 2026, do not deploy product briefs, content briefs, or campaign briefs that tell influencers exactly what to say; let content creators do what they are expert at and create content that gets views.
